title: A & D Precision Ltd. (May 2016 TCC) Tax Court Ruling
subject: Earlier Tax Court proceeding involving A&D Precision Ltd.'s SR&ED claims and procedural or evidentiary issues.
outcome: Ruling issued; court addressed preliminary matters governing the taxpayer's SR&ED appeal.
summary: In A & D Precision Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, the Tax Court of Canada dismissed the Crown's 2016 motion to compel discovery, particulars and admissions in an SR&ED appeal by an Ontario manufacturer. Justice Miller held that SR&ED appeals are a special type of case requiring expert evidence, and that the Respondent knew the case to meet.
metaDescription: Examine the May 2016 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision for A & D Precision Ltd. and its impact on Canadian R&D tax claims.

body.text: (1) Executive Summary & Case Background

The litigation before the Tax Court of Canada in A & D Precision Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, Court File No. 2014-3465(IT)G, represents a defining intersection between procedural tax litigation mechanics and the substantive evidentiary thresholds governing Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives in Canada. The dispute generated two distinct judicial milestones within the same General Procedure docket: first, the interlocutory Oral Reasons for Decision rendered by the Honourable Mr. Justice Campbell J. Miller from the bench at the Federal Judicial Centre in Toronto on May 5, 2016, and signed at Ottawa on June 6, 2016; and second, the subsequent trial on the substantive technical merits heard in Toronto before the Honourable Justice B. Russell over multiple sittings between June 5, 2017 and May 4, 2018, culminating in the judgment rendered on February 28, 2019 and cited as A & D Precision Limited v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2019 TCC 48. Examined in tandem, these decisions illuminate how the Tax Court of Canada delineates the boundary between pre-trial disclosure obligations during examinations for discovery and the rigorous substantive burden of proving technological uncertainty and systematic investigation at trial.
The Taxpayer's Claim and Operational Context

The Appellant, A & D Precision Limited (styled interchangeably in the Tax Court record as A & D Precision Ltd.), is a Canadian privately owned corporation based in Concord, Ontario, whose core business during the fiscal periods at issue was the manufacture of complex, high-precision components for gas turbines and large, complex electrical motors, principally for its primary customer, General Electric Co. (GE). Across multiple taxation years, the Appellant filed prescribed Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) schedules seeking to deduct qualified SR&ED expenditures and claim corresponding Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) in respect of projects it had been working on since the late 1990s, such as the large scale precision vertical lathes project described in its list of documents. To substantiate the technical eligibility of its claimed expenditures, the Appellant submitted narrative documents with its T661 forms described by the Court as copies of "science reports titled SR&ED expenditures by A&D Precision," covering project description, scientific and technological advances, and uncertainties and steps to resolve the uncertainties. Significantly, the Appellant had claimed SR&ED credits for many years, its claims were not challenged following a 2001 SR&ED audit, and it was not until the 2006, 2007 and 2008 taxation years under appeal that the Appellant was denied SR&ED credits on several of the same projects which had previously been accepted.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Following audit verification and administrative objection review, the Minister of National Revenue (the Respondent, acting through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)) reassessed the Appellant's fiscal periods ending June 30, 2006, 2007 and 2008, denying SR&ED credits on several of the same projects which had previously been accepted (investment tax credits totalling 1,212,213 dollars were in issue at trial). The Crown's challenge proceeded along both substantive technical grounds and procedural discovery fronts. On the substantive merits, the trial was confined to the science question of whether the work constituted SR&ED, and the Respondent submitted, for example, that if the welded-steel structure of the Appellant's 80 ton Matteo horizontal lathe and the inertia and deflection caused by the unprecedented weight and length of its workpieces gave rise to technological uncertainties, those uncertainties were overcome by the Appellant using known solutions.

On the procedural front, during the pre-trial discovery phase of Docket 2014-3465(IT)G, the Respondent contended that she did not know the case to meet, having sought to tie the Appellant's technician down to answering questions framed in the language of the Income Tax Act and to be pointed to specific documents showing, for example, a hypothesis or systematic investigation. Consequently, the Respondent took what Justice Miller characterized as a "three-prong approach" in response to what the Crown interpreted as refusals by the Appellant to disclose its case, before bringing the interlocutory motion on which Justice Miller delivered oral reasons on May 5, 2016. First, the Respondent sought to revisit the examinations for discovery of the Appellant's technical representative, who had already been examined for three days, in order to obtain answers to questions refused on discovery. Second, the Respondent served a demand for particulars, again cast in the language of the Act, requiring the Appellant to provide for each project particulars of the work undertaken with respect to, for example, any investigation conducted in a systematic fashion regarding the advancement of scientific knowledge in general without a specific practical use in mind. Third, the Respondent served a Request to Admit, to which the Appellant responded with a blanket denial; the Respondent's ensuing motion then went beyond a standard refusals motion by seeking, first, dismissal of the appeal with costs on the basis that certain paragraphs of the Notice of Appeal were an abuse of process and that the alleged discovery failures warranted dismissal under Rule 110(b), and, in the alternative, orders directing re-attendance at discovery, responses to the request to admit and the demand for particulars, the striking of paragraphs 18, 33 and/or 34 of the Notice of Appeal, the removal of documents from the Appellant's list of documents, and leave to file an amended reply.
The Governing Canadian Statutory and Judicial Framework

The legal dispute in A & D Precision Ltd. is governed exclusively by the federal Income Tax Act (Canada), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA"), the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945), and the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) (SOR/90-688a). The substantive threshold of eligibility rests upon the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which requires a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. For precision manufacturing and machining claimants, eligibility turns on paragraph 248(1)(c) ("experimental development"), which encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Crucially, subsection 248(1) expressly excludes routine data collection, quality control, routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes, commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, and style changes.

Working in concert with subsection 248(1), section 37 of the ITA and Regulation 2900 govern the deductibility and pooling of current SR&ED expenditures, while subsection 37(11) mandates that the taxpayer file prescribed Form T661 containing prescribed project and expenditure information within twelve months of the corporation's filing-due date for the taxation year. In turn, subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA govern the calculation of refundable and non-refundable ITCs (with the refundable portion determined under section 127.1) based on the taxpayer's "qualified expenditure" pool, requiring mandatory reductions for any government assistance, non-government assistance, or "contract payments" received in respect of the SR&ED.

To determine whether a taxpayer's activities satisfy subsection 248(1) of the ITA, the Tax Court of Canada applies the five criteria identified by Bowman J. (as he then was) to assist in determining whether a taxpayer's activities constitute SR&ED, as set out in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, and endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in CW Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, and RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087. Under the Northwest Hydraulic framework, the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that: first, there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard practice; second, the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; third, the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; fourth, the process resulted in a technological advancement; and fifth, a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed, a criterion that Justice Russell described at trial as a factor the presence of which is indicative of the scientific methodology. Procedurally, before an appeal reaches trial on the Northwest Hydraulic criteria, Rules 91, 95, 107, and 110 of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) govern the permissible scope of examinations for discovery and the remedies available when a party refuses to answer proper questions.
The Court's Final Holding

In the Oral Reasons for Decision rendered on May 5, 2016, and signed on June 6, 2016, Justice Campbell J. Miller dismissed the Respondent's interlocutory motion in its entirety and directed that any representations with respect to costs be made within 30 days of the order, failing which costs would be awarded to the Appellant in accordance with the Court's tariff. Justice Miller noted that while interlocutory motions seeking answers to questions refused on discovery are not uncommon, the Crown's motion went further by also seeking orders requiring responses to its demand for particulars and request to admit facts, and went even further by seeking dismissal of the Appellant's appeal altogether based on these alleged failures, although, having heard argument on the other items, Justice Miller found it unnecessary to entertain argument on the request to dismiss. Central to Justice Miller's reasoning was the recognition that "SR&ED appeals are a special type of case". Justice Miller rejected the Respondent's position that she did not know the case to meet: the case had been explained in detail in the science report, the Respondent had received detailed documents properly broken down by project and by activity, had examined the Appellant's technician for three days, had several years' history of following the Appellant's applications relating to the same projects, and had at least three CRA research technical advisors review the projects; he therefore found no need for further examinations, answers, particulars or admissions, concluded that the parties were at the stage to retain experts and move on, and encouraged a settlement conference with the experts in attendance.

The procedural outcome secured by A & D Precision Ltd. in May 2016 was followed by a lengthy trial on the merits before Justice B. Russell, heard in Toronto over multiple sittings between June 5, 2017 and May 4, 2018, and decided on February 28, 2019 (2019 TCC 48). While the Appellant's science reports, its detailed documents broken down by project and by activity, and three days of discovery of its technician were sufficient to defeat the Respondent's interlocutory motion, at trial the Appellant still had to establish that its work satisfied the Northwest Hydraulic criteria, which it did in large part through drawings, engineering calculations and the testimony of its fact witnesses, notably its founder and president Antranik Derbedrosian and its chief engineer, the late George Predoiu. The Appellant called two university-affiliated experts with advanced expertise in machine tool design and testing, Drs. Stephen Veldhuis and Eu-Gene Ng, the Respondent called Dr. Yusuf Altintas, and Justice Russell found their evidence of general assistance; the Court allowed the appeal in part, without costs due to divided success, finding that the work on the 80 ton Matteo horizontal lathe (Project #4) and on the double wheel roll grinding machine (Project #6) constituted SR&ED, while denying the Project #4 claims relating to the three purchased Tacchi lathes (2006 fiscal period) and to the 60 and 40 ton Matteo lathes (two-thirds of the 2008 Project #4 claim), applying the criteria in Northwest Hydraulic.
(2) Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

A comprehensive legal and technical review of Docket 2014-3465(IT)G—encompassing both the May 2016 discovery ruling and the subsequent trial decision—identifies five areas of substantiation, methodology, documentation, and procedural management that determined which portions of the SR&ED claims were disallowed and which were allowed.
Failure to Distinguish Technological Uncertainty from Routine Precision Machining and Standard Practice

The foundational threshold of any Canadian SR&ED claim under subsection 248(1) of the ITA and the first criterion of Northwest Hydraulic is the existence of "technological uncertainty"—defined in Canadian tax jurisprudence as either a fundamental system uncertainty or a capability limitation within the underlying body of scientific or technological knowledge that cannot be resolved through standard practice or routine engineering. In A & D Precision Ltd., the Court found a technological (system) uncertainty in the design and build of the 80 ton Matteo lathe and a technical uncertainty in the novel double wheel roll grinding machine, but found no non-trivial system uncertainty for the 60 and 40 ton Matteo lathes, which were in large part simply smaller versions of the 80 ton Matteo built in accordance with conventional design.

Within the custom machining and tooling industry, holding sub-micron geometric tolerances, achieving mirror surface finishes, maximizing material removal rates, and suppressing harmonic tool chatter or premature insert wear are everyday commercial engineering challenges. A & D Precision Ltd. described the uncertainties in its projects and the steps taken to resolve them in the science reports filed with its T661 forms, and at trial characterized the uncertainty in designing and building the 80 ton Matteo lathe as a system uncertainty arising from the non-trivial combination of known technologies. However, Canadian jurisprudence draws an uncompromising line between a difficult commercial or technical problem and true technological uncertainty. When a skilled machinist or manufacturing engineer addresses dimensional non-conformance or tool deflection by adjusting spindle speeds, feed rates, depths of cut, coolant delivery pressures, tool coatings, or workholding fixtures within parameters known or readily determinable by competent professionals in the field, the work constitutes "routine engineering".

At trial, the Appellant introduced expert testimony from two university-affiliated experts with advanced expertise in machine tool design and testing, Drs. Stephen Veldhuis and Eu-Gene Ng, while the Respondent's expert, Dr. Yusuf Altintas, acknowledged that system uncertainty could constitute a technological uncertainty. While academic experts can explain the complex thermo-mechanical, tribological, and metallurgical phenomena occurring within the shear zone of a cutting tool, Justice Russell described the experts' evidence as being of general assistance, and the outcome of each claim turned principally on the testimony of the Appellant's fact witnesses and the supporting drawings and engineering calculations. The threshold requirement of technological uncertainty was not met for the 60 and 40 ton Matteo lathes, whose cast-iron construction, off-the-shelf spindle bearings and ball-screw z-axis drive were in accord with conventional horizontal lathe design, and the Appellant offered no basis for its 2006 claim relating to the three purchased Tacchi lathes; by contrast, the Court found a system uncertainty for the 80 ton Matteo and a technical uncertainty for the novel double wheel roll grinding machine.
Absence of a Structured Process of Systematic Experimentation and Hypothesis Testing

Under the second and third criteria of Northwest Hydraulic, a claimant must formulate specific, testable hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating the identified technological uncertainty and must test those hypotheses through a systematic investigation governed by the scientific method. In the A & D Precision Ltd. litigation, Justice Russell was satisfied that Mr. Predoiu, with Mr. Derbedrosian, formulated theories or plans (which could be termed hypotheses) to minimize the risks of system uncertainty and vibration, and that the 80 ton Matteo and grinding machine projects accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, even though the 80 ton Matteo was tested after assembly rather than through prototypes, which would have been cost-prohibitive.

In a systematic scientific investigation, the practitioner observes a failure mode that defies standard practice, formulates a specific causal hypothesis explaining the physical mechanism driving that failure, designs a controlled experiment that isolates the independent variables while holding boundary conditions constant, measures the dependent physical outcomes quantitatively, and modifies the hypothesis based on rigorous analytical evaluation of the results. By contrast, in commercial precision machining environments, operators under production deadlines routinely adjust multiple variables simultaneously—such as swapping a carbide insert geometry while concurrently modifying the CNC toolpath strategy and feed rate—with the sole objective of producing a dimensionally conforming part. While such heuristic troubleshooting is commercially effective, the Tax Court of Canada consistently rules that ad-hoc trial-and-error adjustments lack the methodological discipline required to constitute "experiment or analysis" under subsection 248(1) of the ITA.
Reliance on Post-Hoc T661 "Science Reports" Over Contemporaneous Documentation

A critical evidentiary insight emerging from Justice Miller's May 2016 ruling and the ensuing trial in Docket 2014-3465(IT)G concerns the sharp divergence between the procedural utility and the substantive probative value of narrative "science reports" filed with Form T661. As Justice Miller noted in the May 5, 2016 Oral Reasons for Decision, the Appellant submitted with its T661 forms copies of "science reports titled SR&ED". In Canadian tax compliance practice, corporate taxpayers frequently engage external SR&ED consultants or internal technical writers after the close of the fiscal year to draft narrative technical reports supplementing Part 2 of Form T661.

In the May 2016 interlocutory proceeding, the existence of these science reports, together with the Appellant's detailed documents broken down by project and by activity, three days of discovery of its technician, and the Respondent's years of history with the same projects, assisted A & D Precision Ltd. in defeating the Crown's motion, because they gave the Respondent sufficient knowledge of the case to meet (Justice Miller found it unnecessary to hear argument on the request to dismiss the appeal). At trial, however, the Appellant's proof of experimentation rested not on post-hoc narrative science reports or expert reconstructions but on drawings, engineering calculations and fulsome witness testimony, which Justice Russell assessed under the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic. That criterion, which Justice Russell described as a factor the presence of which is indicative of the scientific methodology, contemplates that a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results achieved be kept as the work progresses. Narrative science reports drafted months after the taxation year-end without an underlying foundation of dated shop-floor test matrices, coordinate measuring machine (CMM) metrological inspection logs tied to specific experimental runs, scrap analysis records, and contemporaneous engineering notebooks carry limited evidentiary weight on their own; in A & D Precision, however, records kept largely in the form of drawings of many if not most significant parts, together with engineering calculations and fulsome testimony, were found sufficient for the 80 ton Matteo and the grinding machine, even though it was acknowledged that few records pertaining to the testing protocol itself were made or retained.
Multi-Year Project Rollover and Expenditure Allocation Deficiencies

In the May 5, 2016 ruling, Justice Miller noted that the Appellant's SR&ED claims, which had not been challenged following a 2001 SR&ED audit, were not challenged until the 2006, 2007 and 2008 taxation years, for which the Appellant was denied credits on several of the same projects which had previously been accepted, and that the Respondent had several years' history of following the Appellant's applications relating to the same projects. This factual element illustrates a compliance risk in multi-year manufacturing SR&ED claims, namely the rollover of project narratives and claimed technological uncertainties across consecutive taxation years; at trial, Justice Russell analysed Project #4 separately for each fiscal period (the Tacchi lathes in 2006, the 80 ton Matteo in 2007, and all three Matteo lathes without any allocation in 2008), while allowing Project #6 in all three fiscal periods.

Under the Canadian statutory regime, each taxation year stands as an isolated evidentiary unit. When a taxpayer claims the same machining or tooling project across multiple fiscal years without documenting how the technological baseline advanced at the conclusion of Year 1 and what distinct, residual, or newly discovered technological uncertainties arose in Year 2, the claim for each year must nonetheless be supported on its own facts; in A & D Precision, the Court allowed the multi-year Project #6 claim in full for all three fiscal periods, but where the Appellant claimed three Matteo lathes in 2008 without any allocation of expenses among them, the Court allocated one-third to each and allowed only the one-third relating to the 80 ton Matteo. Moreover, when precision machining is performed in a dual-use commercial facility—where identical CNC machinery, operators, and raw bar stock or castings are used for both commercial customer orders and purported SR&ED—failing to maintain contemporaneous time-tracking and cost-segregation records connecting specific labour hours and material consumption to discrete experimental hypotheses exposes the financial expenditure claim under subsections 37(1) and 127(9) of the ITA to challenge, although in A & D Precision it was agreed or decided at trial that only the science question was in issue and the financial questions, such as the hours claimed and the non-scientific elements of shared-use equipment, had not been put in issue.
Procedural Discovery Friction and Commercial Contract / Funded Research Boundaries

The May 2016 interlocutory ruling also illustrates the strategic hazards created when a taxpayer's pre-trial discovery posture collides with its substantive burden of proof. During examinations for discovery, the Crown sought to tie the Appellant's technician down to answering questions framed in the language of the Income Tax Act and to be pointed to specific documents showing, for example, a hypothesis or systematic investigation. When the Appellant responded that its technician had described all of the work done and that it would be for experts to answer such questions, the Crown pursued its three-prong approach of revisiting examinations, serving a demand for particulars and serving a Request to Admit, and then moved to compel re-attendance and to dismiss the appeal.

Although Justice Miller dismissed the Crown's interlocutory motion—holding that SR&ED appeals are a special type of case that demand the assistance of experts, and that the Appellant was a taxpayer with a legitimate claim to be adjudicated who had proffered all the relevant factual background, simply not in the manner the Respondent would prefer—it remains critical for an appellant to provide the factual underpinnings for expert evidence to be of any use, and at trial the claims for which the Appellant offered little evidence or explanation, notably the 2006 expenditures relating to the Tacchi lathes, were denied, while those supported by drawings, calculations and testimony were allowed. Furthermore, in precision machining and custom tooling operations, projects almost invariably originate from commercial customer purchase orders or fixed-price supply agreements. Under subsections 127(9) and 127(11.1) of the ITA, if a customer contract obligates the manufacturer to perform development work or reimburses tooling and prototype expenses, the customer's payments risk characterization as a "contract payment" that reduces the taxpayer's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar. To preserve ITC eligibility, the taxpayer must prove through clear contractual provisions that it was contracted strictly to deliver a commercial product at its own financial risk and undertook the underlying process SR&ED independently while retaining ownership of the resulting manufacturing process intellectual property.
(3) Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory, judicial, and procedural requirement examined in the A & D Precision Ltd. litigation (encompassing the May 2016 Interlocutory Decision in Docket 2014-3465(IT)G and the subsequent Trial Decision in 2019 TCC 48) against the taxpayer's specific deficiencies or successes as found by the Court and the governing standard of proof enforced by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof

cells: 1. Technological Uncertainty
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 1

Established a system uncertainty for the 80 ton Matteo lathe and a technical uncertainty for the novel double wheel roll grinding machine, but showed no non-trivial system uncertainty for the 60 and 40 ton Matteo lathes, whose differences were in accord with conventional horizontal lathe design; the experts' evidence was of general assistance to the Court.

Taxpayer must prove through objective, baseline-establishing evidence that a system uncertainty or capability gap existed that could not be resolved by a competent professional using standard engineering practice or publicly available knowledge.
2. Formulation of Hypotheses
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 2

For the 80 ton Matteo and the grinding machine, the Court accepted that Mr. Predoiu, with Mr. Derbedrosian, formulated theories or plans (which could be termed hypotheses) to minimize the risks of system uncertainty and vibration.

Taxpayer must demonstrate that each experimental iteration was preceded by a specific, testable hypothesis identifying the causal relationship between independent technological variables and the observed failure mode.
3. Systematic Investigation & Experimentation
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 3

The Court found that the 80 ton Matteo and grinding machine work accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, although the 80 ton Matteo was tested after assembly rather than through prototypes, whose cost would have been prohibitive.

Taxpayer must prove adherence to the scientific method: systematic observation, hypothesis formulation, controlled testing, quantitative measurement of outcomes, and iterative modification of hypotheses based on data analysis.
4. Technological Advancement
ITA s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 4

The Court found that the 80 ton Matteo represented a step forward, however incremental, in general technical knowledge, and that the abandoned grinding machine project achieved technological advancement even though it was ended before any successful outcome.

Taxpayer must establish that the investigation generated new technological knowledge that advances the understanding of the underlying technology for skilled practitioners, even if the physical prototype ultimately failed.
5. Contemporaneous Documentation
Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 5; ITA s. 230(1)

Records were kept largely in the form of drawings of many if not most significant parts, supported by engineering calculations, although few records of the testing protocol itself were made or retained; supplemented by fulsome testimony, this was found sufficient for the 80 ton Matteo and the grinding machine.

The fifth criterion is a factor whose presence is indicative of the scientific methodology; the taxpayer should produce dated, contemporaneous records generated during the execution of the SR&ED (e.g., test matrices, CMM metrology logs, engineering notes) recording the hypotheses tested and results observed in real time.
6. Multi-Year Project Differentiation
ITA ss. 37(1), 248(1); A & D Precision (May 2016)

Claimed SR&ED credits for many years on projects worked on since the late 1990s, which were not challenged until credits were denied for the 2006, 2007 and 2008 taxation years on several of the same projects previously accepted; at trial, the 2008 Project #4 claim covered three Matteo lathes without any allocation, so the Court allocated one-third to each.

Each taxation year stands alone; for multi-year projects, the taxpayer must prove the exact technological state at the start of the fiscal year and prove that the current year's work addressed new or unresolved technological uncertainties.
7. Pre-Trial Discovery & Case Disclosure
Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) Rules 91, 95, 107, 110

Declined, on discovery, questions framed in the language of the ITA and requests to identify specific documents showing hypotheses or systematic investigation, declined the demand for particulars and gave a blanket denial to the Request to Admit, maintaining that it had provided everything it could and that experts would address qualification; the Crown then moved to compel answers and dismiss the appeal.

Under Justice Miller's May 2016 ruling, SR&ED appeals are a "special type of case": they demand the assistance of experts, and although it remains critical to provide the factual underpinnings for expert evidence, the motion was dismissed because the science report, documents broken down by project and activity, three days of discovery and years of history with the same projects meant the Respondent knew the case to meet.
8. Expenditure Segregation & Contract Exclusion
ITA ss. 37(1), 127(9), 127(11.1); Form T661
Not adjudicated: the financial questions (such as the hours claimed and the non-scientific elements of shared-use equipment) were not put in issue at trial, which addressed only the science question.

Taxpayer must maintain verifiable time-tracking and cost accounting segregating eligible SR&ED activities (directly attributable or incremental) from commercial production and prove no reduction via "contract payments".

body.text: (4) Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial principles established in A & D Precision Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen (spanning both the May 2016 procedural discovery ruling and the 2019 TCC 48 substantive trial judgment) into rigorous compliance frameworks, the following two applied Canadian industry case studies examine realistic industrial projects vulnerable to the pitfalls illustrated by the disallowed portions of the claims and the discovery dispute in Docket 2014-3465(IT)G. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how the taxpayer can restructure its project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking to overcome the Tax Court's objections and satisfy all statutory SR&ED requirements under the ITA.
Case Study 1: Aerospace Precision Multi-Axis CNC Machining of Thin-Walled Titanium-Aluminide Components
Baseline Scenario and Exposure to A & D Precision Ltd. Pitfalls

AeroMachining Ontario Inc. ("AeroMachining"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) headquartered in Mississauga, Ontario, specializes in manufacturing high-precision aerospace turbine components. AeroMachining enters into a commercial supply agreement with a Tier-1 aerospace prime contractor to deliver 500 thin-walled gamma titanium-aluminide (γ-TiAl) low-pressure turbine casings requiring wall thicknesses of 0.85 mm ± 0.012 mm and a surface roughness of Ra ≤ 0.4 µm. During initial production runs on its 5-axis CNC machining centers, AeroMachining experiences severe harmonic tool chatter, micro-cracking along the intermetallic grain boundaries, and thermal distortion exceeding 0.08 mm upon fixture release. Over a two-year period, shop-floor machinists adjust spindle speeds, test different polycrystalline diamond (PCD) and coated carbide inserts recommended by tooling vendors, and modify G-code toolpaths until acceptable parts are produced. At the conclusion of each fiscal year, AeroMachining retains an external SR&ED consultant who prepares a 25-page narrative "Science Report" attached to Form T661 claiming $850,000 in machinist wages and scrap materials across both fiscal years. No formal experimental logs are kept on the shop floor, and machinist labour hours are billed globally to the customer job number.

If audited by the CRA and litigated before the Tax Court of Canada, AeroMachining faces vulnerabilities similar to those that led to the disallowed portions of the taxpayer's claims in A & D Precision Ltd.. The year-end T661 "Science Report" represents a post-hoc narrative reconstruction devoid of contemporaneous shop-floor evidence. Testing vendor-recommended inserts and adjusting G-code parameters appears indistinguishable from routine CNC optimization rather than resolving a fundamental technological uncertainty. Furthermore, claiming the same project across two consecutive taxation years without distinct annual baselines invites disallowed multi-year rollover challenges, while global job-order time tracking blends commercial production with experimental trials, creating severe pre-trial discovery vulnerabilities under Rule 95 of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance and Pre-Project Baseline Gatekeeping

Before claiming any shop-floor activity as SR&ED, AeroMachining must establish a formal SR&ED Technical Governance Committee comprising its Lead Manufacturing Engineer, Chief Metallurgist, and Corporate Controller. When the initial γ-TiAl machining failures occur, the governance protocol mandates that the engineering team first compile a formal Standard Practice Exhaustion Report prior to initiating an SR&ED project. This baseline report documents all standard CNC machining adjustments attempted—including vendor-specified cutting speeds of 35 to 50 m/min, standard high-pressure through-spindle coolant at 70 bar, and conventional trochoidal milling toolpaths—and demonstrates quantitatively why established engineering methods failed to prevent subsurface intermetallic cleavage and thermal springback.

Only after documenting the exhaustion of standard practice does the committee authorize a formal SR&ED Project Initiation Charter. The charter explicitly defines the governing Technological Uncertainty in terms of underlying materials science and machining mechanics: specifically, that existing thermo-mechanical machining models cannot predict the coupled residual stress distribution and brittle-to-ductile transition behaviour in thin-walled γ-TiAl castings when dynamic fixture damping and cryogenic minimum-quantity lubrication (MQL) interact at high strain rates. To address the multi-year claim history noted by Justice Miller in the May 2016 A & D Precision Ltd. ruling, the governance charter enforces a mandatory technical cut-off at the close of Fiscal Year 1. The Year 1 project file must close with an audited technical statement establishing the exact technological advancement achieved during that fiscal period—such as resolving intermetallic micro-cracking through a novel ultrasonic-assisted cryogenic cutting regime—and defining a newly elevated technological baseline and a distinct technological uncertainty for Fiscal Year 2, such as resolving harmonic fixture resonance induced by the ultrasonic spindle transducer in the second year.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous Evidence Architecture

To eliminate reliance on retrospective year-end T661 "science reports", AeroMachining must embed real-time documentation directly into its shop-floor Manufacturing Execution System (MES). Under this restructured protocol, no experimental machining trial can be executed on a CNC machining center without first generating a time-stamped digital Hypothesis-Experiment-Result (HER) Card in the MES prior to cycle start. Each HER Card compels the supervising engineer to record three mandatory pre-test elements before the spindle engages: first, the specific causal hypothesis being tested (for example, testing the proposition that applying liquid nitrogen cryogenic jet cooling at −196°C exclusively to the tool flank face while maintaining dry rake-face cutting will localize thermal softening in the primary shear zone while preventing tensile residual stress gradients in the 0.85 mm wall); second, the controlled independent variables (nozzle impingement angle, mass flow rate, tool rake angle, cutting velocity v<sub>c</sub>, and feed per tooth f<sub>z</sub>); and third, the quantitative pass/fail metrics.

Each experimental workpiece is laser-marked with a unique serialized identifier (such as EXP-FY26-TIAL-014) prior to machining. During and immediately following the trial run, multi-component piezoelectric spindle dynamometer cutting-force logs (Fx, Fy, Fz), acoustic emission frequency spectra, CMM dimensional deviation maps, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) metallographic cross-sections are automatically linked to that serialized workpiece identifier within an immutable, version-controlled engineering database. This real-time data architecture satisfies the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic by ensuring that a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results achieved is generated contemporaneously as the work progresses.
Step 3: Commercial Contract Terms and Financial Risk Allocation

To prevent the CRA from recharacterizing the aerospace customer supply agreement as "contracted SR&ED" or reducing AeroMachining's qualified expenditure pool via "contract payments" under subsections 127(9) and 127(11.1) of the ITA, AeroMachining must restructure its contractual documentation prior to project execution. The supply agreement with the Tier-1 aerospace prime contractor must be drafted strictly as a fixed-price commercial contract for the sale of goods (500 conforming turbine casings at a fixed unit price), containing no covenant obligating AeroMachining to perform R&D services, engineering hours, or experimental trials on the customer's behalf.

Furthermore, the contract must incorporate an explicit Intellectual Property Retention Clause stipulating that while the aerospace customer retains title to the physical component geometry (the part blueprint), AeroMachining retains 100 percent exclusive legal and beneficial ownership of all manufacturing processes, custom tooling geometries, cryogenic delivery architectures, and CNC control algorithms developed during performance of the contract. Finally, contractual payment milestones must be conditioned strictly upon the delivery and acceptance of dimensionally conforming commercial hardware meeting AS9100 aerospace quality standards, demonstrating unequivocally that AeroMachining bears the full financial risk of all failed experimental iterations.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking, Cost Segregation, and Discovery Readiness

To avoid the type of dispute over alleged discovery refusals addressed in the May 2016 decision of Justice Miller, AeroMachining must reconfigure its Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and payroll accounting systems to enforce strict activity segregation. The ERP system is programmed to separate commercial production job codes (such as PROD-4001) from experimental SR&ED sub-codes tied directly to specific HER Card sequences (such as SRED-EXP-1.1 through SRED-EXP-1.8). Shop-floor machinists and manufacturing engineers badge into the SR&ED sub-codes exclusively during the setup, execution, teardown, and metrological analysis of authorized HER Card trials, automatically halting SR&ED time accumulation the moment the machine resumes commercial production runs.

Concurrently, any experimental trial casting that is destructively sectioned for metallographic inspection or rendered unusable due to experimental parameter testing is logged in a dedicated SR&ED Scrap and Material Consumed Register supported by photographic and weight verification, rigorously distinguishing materials "consumed" versus materials "transformed" under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the ITA. At the conclusion of each taxation year, AeroMachining compiles a comprehensive Pre-Audit and Discovery Binder that cross-references every dollar claimed on Form T661 directly to specific payroll timesheets, ERP material vouchers, and time-stamped HER Cards. Should the claim ever proceed to an examination for discovery under Rule 95 in the Tax Court of Canada, AeroMachining's corporate nominee can answer every factual and financial linkage inquiry thoroughly and without refusals, neutralizing any basis for a Crown motion while building an unassailable evidentiary foundation for trial.
Case Study 2: Custom Automated Progressive Die and High-Speed Micro-Assembly System Integration
Baseline Scenario and Exposure to A & D Precision Ltd. Pitfalls

PrecisionTooling Systems Ltd. ("PrecisionTooling"), a custom automation and precision die manufacturer located in Windsor, Ontario, is contracted by a medical device corporation to design and build a high-speed automated progressive stamping die integrated with a robotic laser-welding micro-assembly cell. The system is required to stamp and laser-weld 316L surgical stainless steel sleeves to Nitinol (nickel-titanium shape-memory alloy) micro-catheter actuator wires at 400 strokes per minute (SPM) with zero burr formation and weld positional accuracy of ±3 µm. During shop-floor integration and commissioning, PrecisionTooling encounters severe Nitinol pseudo-elastic springback variability across the progressive die stations and catastrophic brittle intermetallic phase formation (Ti2Ni and Fe2Ti) at the laser weld interface between the Nitinol wire and the 316L stainless steel sleeve. Over a 14-month period, toolmakers re-grind die punches, adjust servo-press motion profiles, and modify fiber-laser pulse durations directly on the assembly line until the system passes Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) and is shipped to the customer. PrecisionTooling claims $1.2 million in SR&ED expenditures on Form T661, submitting a narrative "Science Report" prepared by an external consultant that characterizes the entire 14-month machine build and debugging phase as a single unified SR&ED project. During the CRA audit and subsequent Tax Court discovery, PrecisionTooling's nominee is unable to produce shop-floor experimental logs and refuses to break down how much labour time was devoted to standard mechanical frame assembly versus experimental laser and forming trials.

Under the legal framework applied in A & D Precision Ltd., PrecisionTooling faces severe disqualification exposure. Claiming an entire commercial machine build alongside routine shop-floor debugging and FAT commissioning violates the statutory exclusion for commercial production and routine engineering under subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Because the custom automated system is sold as commercial property to the medical device client, claiming the whole build conflates commercial Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) with deductible SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) and exposes the claim to "contract payment" reductions under subsection 127(9). Moreover, the external T661 "Science Report" improperly aggregates routine computer-aided design (CAD) drafting, standard CNC machining of base plates, and electrical panel wiring with genuine technological experimentation, while refusing to disaggregate those activities during discovery invites a Crown three-prong approach (revisiting examinations, a demand for particulars and a Request to Admit) followed by a motion for re-attendance and dismissal.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance and Architectural Decomposition

PrecisionTooling must immediately abandon the "whole-machine claim" methodology and institute a Sub-System Decomposition Governance Model supervised by an internal R&D Steering Committee. At the project inception milestone, the engineering team decomposes the custom automated line into discrete functional assemblies. All sub-systems relying on established engineering practice—including the structural steel machine frame, safety light curtains, standard programmable logic controller (PLC) conveyor sequencing, and off-the-shelf pneumatic pick-and-place modules—are classified from day one as 100 percent Commercial Engineering and excluded from the SR&ED claim scope.

Only the specific sub-systems confronting genuine technological capability barriers that cannot be resolved through standard mechanical or metallurgical engineering are carved out as authorized SR&ED sub-projects. Specifically, the Steering Committee charters Sub-Project A to investigate High-Strain-Rate Adiabatic Forming of Superelastic Nitinol at 400 SPM (aimed at resolving non-linear stress-induced martensitic phase transformation and elastic recovery hysteresis), and charters Sub-Project B to investigate Dissimilar Ultra-Short-Pulse Laser Micro-Welding of Nitinol to 316L Stainless Steel (aimed at suppressing brittle Ti<sub>x</sub>Ni<sub>y</sub>Fe<sub>z</sub> intermetallic phase nucleation within a < 15 millisecond cycle window). The governance protocol enforces a strict Phase-Gate Termination Rule: the moment the experimental forming and laser-welding parameters are validated and transferred to the final machine build for routine integration and Factory Acceptance Testing, the SR&ED project codes are permanently closed.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous Evidence Architecture

To replace retrospective T661 "science reports" with unimpeachable contemporaneous evidence, PrecisionTooling physically and documentarily isolates its experimental investigations from commercial assembly by constructing an offline single-station experimental die test rig and a benchtop laser-welding test cell. Rather than conducting unrecorded trial-and-error adjustments on the customer's production machine, the welding metallurgist and forming engineers execute structured Design of Experiments (DoE) matrices on the offline test rigs.

For Sub-Project B, the team establishes a fractional factorial DoE matrix systematically testing hypotheses regarding spatial ring-mode beam shaping, picosecond-to-nanosecond pulse modulation, and thin-film vanadium/nickel interlayer diffusion barriers. Every experimental run in the DoE matrix is entered contemporaneously into a Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) prior to testing. Each welded micro-coupon is subsequently subjected to quantitative destructive and non-destructive testing, including micro-tensile pull testing, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) elemental mapping, and micro-Vickers hardness profiling across the fusion zone. The raw instrumental outputs, metallurgical micrographs, and engineering interpretations—explicitly documenting failed hypotheses and how each failure informed the formulation of the subsequent hypothesis—are cryptographically time-stamped and archived weekly in the LIMS repository in strict compliance with Northwest Hydraulic.
Step 3: Commercial Contract Terms and Custom Equipment Structuring

Because PrecisionTooling sells the completed automated assembly system to its medical device customer, disciplined contractual structuring is essential to protect the claim against "contract payment" reductions under subsection 127(9) of the ITA and commercial asset exclusions. PrecisionTooling must structure its customer contract strictly as a fixed-price commercial agreement for the sale of a turnkey capital piece of manufacturing equipment, ensuring that the contract contains no terms engaging PrecisionTooling to perform research and development services for or on behalf of the customer.

The contract must incorporate an explicit Background and Foreground Intellectual Property Clause under which the customer acquires title solely to the physical machinery delivered and a non-exclusive license to operate that machinery for catheter production, while PrecisionTooling retains exclusive legal ownership of all foreground patents, trade secrets, pulse-shaping algorithms, and adiabatic die-station kinematics generated during Sub-Projects A and B. Simultaneously, in its tax accounting schedules, PrecisionTooling excludes all structural components, servo drives, PLC hardware, and laser sources incorporated into the shipped commercial machine from its Form T661 material expenditure claim, treating those items strictly as commercial COGS. Only the sacrificial Nitinol wire, 316L stainless steel test coupons, sacrificial experimental die inserts, and expendable optical elements physically consumed or rendered worthless on the offline test rigs during Sub-Projects A and B are claimed as eligible SR&ED materials under subsection 37(1) of the ITA.
Step 4: Experimentation Tracking, Support Work Capture, and Discovery Readiness

To achieve total audit transparency and eliminate the discovery vulnerabilities addressed in Justice Miller's May 2016 ruling, PrecisionTooling implements granular activity-based time tracking across its engineering and toolmaking workforce. Toolmakers, laser physicists, and control engineers log their hours daily via shop-floor terminals mapped directly to specific LIMS DoE run identifiers (such as DOE-A-Run01 through DOE-B-Run45), accompanied by a mandatory daily technical task log describing the exact experimental procedure executed.

Crucially, engineering tasks that do not themselves constitute direct experimentation—such as machining the custom experimental fixtures required to hold the Nitinol coupons inside the offline test rig, or coding the data-acquisition scripts needed to capture high-speed pyrometric thermal imaging during laser pulse trials—are separately coded under the statutory category of "support work" pursuant to subsection 248(1) of the ITA. The tracking system requires the supervisor to verify and document how each hour of claimed support work falls within the eight statutory categories of support work (engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research) and is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the experimental hypotheses tested in Sub-Projects A and B. At year-end, Part 2 of Form T661 is synthesized directly from the contemporaneous LIMS DoE records rather than fabricated as a post-hoc external "science report," and all supporting timesheets, EDS spectra, and COGS reconciliation schedules are compiled into a Rule 95 Discovery Readiness Ledger. By aligning its operational governance and evidentiary records with the strict requirements of the Income Tax Act and the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure), the taxpayer ensures that its claim can withstand both rigorous pre-trial discovery scrutiny and a full substantive trial on the merits.
